title: HTTP State Management Mechanism
summary: Specifies a second version of HTTP state management (cookies), a way to create stateful sessions with HTTP requests and responses. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 6265.

eli5.summary: Websites use small notes called cookies to remember you. This was a newer design for those notes that did not catch on.

questions: how do cookies work in http
subtitle: A second attempt at HTTP state management using Set-Cookie2 and Cookie headers.

tldr.problem: HTTP is stateless: each request is independent, making it hard to track users through sessions for shopping carts or logins.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2965 defines Set-Cookie2 and Cookie headers to send small pieces of state data between servers and clients. Servers use Set-Cookie2 to send state to clients, and clients return that state in Cookie request headers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides finer control over cookies than the Netscape standard it tried to improve, but Netscape's version dominated in practice. RFC 2965 is now Historic and replaced by RFC 6265.

today: RFC 2965 is Historic, replaced by RFC 6265. While it was a more sophisticated approach to state management than the Netscape specification, that simpler standard became the de facto web standard. RFC 6265 acknowledged this reality and codified how cookies actually work on the modern web, rather than how RFC 2965 specified they should work.

sections.title: Creating Stateful Sessions on the Web
sections.content:
HTTP treats each request independently, so servers do not naturally remember earlier requests from the same client. State management solves this by letting servers send small pieces of information to clients, which the clients then return with subsequent requests. This enables sessions: a sequence of related requests from one client to a server.

RFC 2965 specifies a second version of HTTP state management, improving on RFC 2109 and describing three new HTTP headers: Set-Cookie2 (sent by the server to give state to the client), Cookie (sent by the client to return state), and Cookie2 (sent by the client to advertise which cookie version it understands).
sections.eli5: Imagine talking to a teacher who has no memory between lessons. The teacher could give you a note at the end of class saying, "You talked about dinosaurs today." You bring that note back the next day so the teacher remembers your conversation.

sections.title: Cookies and Their Attributes
sections.content:
A cookie is a small piece of state that a server sends to a client and expects the client to return on future requests. The Set-Cookie2 header sets a cookie with a name, value, and optional attributes. The most important attributes are Domain (which server domains can use the cookie), Path (which request paths should include the cookie), Max-Age (how many seconds the cookie lasts), and Port (which ports the cookie applies to).

Other attributes control privacy and security: Secure means send the cookie only over an encrypted connection, Discard means forget the cookie when the browser closes, and Comment lets the server explain why it wants the cookie. Version identifies which cookie specification the server is using.
sections.eli5: A cookie is like a labeled box. The label says who can open it (Domain), where it belongs (Path), when to throw it away (Max-Age), and whether to keep it secret (Secure).

sections.title: The Cookie Exchange
sections.content:
A cookie session begins when a server sends a Set-Cookie2 response header with a cookie. The client stores this cookie and, on future requests to the same server (or servers that match the cookie's Domain and Path), includes the cookie in a Cookie request header.

The server can update or replace cookies by sending new Set-Cookie2 headers. A cookie with Max-Age=0 tells the client to discard the cookie immediately. The RFC defines rules for which cookies a client should send with each request: the request's host must domain-match the cookie's Domain, the request's path must path-match the cookie's Path, and the request port must match the cookie's Port attribute (if specified).
sections.eli5: The server hands you a note (Set-Cookie2). You carry the note with you (Cookie header). The server might ask for a new note later, or say the old note is no good anymore (Max-Age=0).

sections.title: Privacy and Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Cookies can track users and reveal sensitive information. The RFC restricts where cookies can be sent to limit leakage: a server can only set a cookie for its own domain or a parent domain, and cookies are not sent in unverifiable transactions (like embedded images from third parties) unless the client explicitly allows it.

The Secure attribute tells the client to send a cookie only over an encrypted connection, protecting it from eavesdropping. However, cookies are still in plain text in HTTP responses, so servers SHOULD NOT store sensitive information like passwords in them. The Comment attribute lets servers explain their cookie usage, helping users make informed decisions about whether to accept cookies.
sections.eli5: Cookies could let a website follow you around the web, so the rules say a website can only get the note you carry for that specific website. If a website wants to store something secret, it should use encryption.

sections.title: Version 2 and Why It Lost
sections.content:
RFC 2965 was an improvement over RFC 2109, correcting errors and adding features. However, Netscape's simpler Set-Cookie (v0) specification had already dominated the web. Browsers implemented both old and new-style cookies for backward compatibility, but servers largely stuck with the simpler Set-Cookie header.

RFC 2965 is now Historic. It was superseded by RFC 6265, which cleaned up the spec and acknowledged the reality that Netscape's original design had won. The new RFC also addressed real-world cookie usage patterns that RFC 2965 did not anticipate.
sections.eli5: This RFC tried to make cookies more complicated and safer, but websites and browsers had already learned to use a simpler rule that worked fine. So eventually they wrote down what actually won (RFC 6265) instead of what this RFC said to do.
